The roadmap - what this talk actually answers.

Three quick disclaimers. The code is there to demonstrate the ideas, not production code. Most of the diagrams and code were generated with AI, and I checked them. And I'll show a lot of tools to give the full picture: I'm not an expert in all of them, and I haven't run all of them in production.
The big question. Let it land, then move.
Live demo - the actual dashboard, embedded live from solar_dashboard.py. If it breaks, keep talking and fall back to describing it.
The map for the next few slides: CSVs in, pandas shapes them, Altair draws them, marimo makes it interactive and turns it into these slides. Then we go through each step in code.
Ingestion: one tab per source system - click through them; the code underneath changes with the tab. The readings only name their sensor; the sensors tab says which plant each one is in.

Click: the data model, as a star schema. Facts in blue: the sensor readings, the grid settlement, and daily_plant_performance - one row per plant per day, what the dashboard is built on. Dimensions in lavender: sensors and plants. A reading only names its sensor; the sensor dimension says which plant it is in.
Gold: hourly readings become daily energy, joined to what the grid operator paid - and self-consumption falls out as the difference.
Plotting, step 1: the simplest possible Altair chart - x, y, colour.
Step 2: lines become stacked areas.
Step 3: titles, outline, smooth curves, readable numbers.
Step 4: tooltips - hover the chart.
Filters, step 1: a slider is one line. Move it - the text below updates.
Step 2: a multiselect, everything selected to start.

Step 3: marimo has no date-range slider, so the dashboard uses its own widget - an anywidget: a Python class with a small JavaScript front end and synced state. Defined once, used like any marimo element.

Step 2: the same selection in a second chart - click either chart and both react.
Four services really, dressed up nine ways.
Click through a tab or two live.
The three questions of the talk. The map is the plan for the rest of it: we go through it piece by piece, and every question mark becomes an open-source tool.
The map again, one piece at a time. First: getting the raw data in.

Airbyte copies data in: hundreds of open-source connectors, set up in a UI - pick a source, a destination and a schedule. Incremental syncs and CDC, so each run only moves what changed. For an API without a connector, the Connector Builder makes one without code. Click the dots to flip through the screenshots.
Storage: first how the data sits in files - Parquet, then the table formats on top - then the databases.

Parquet in one slide: a columnar, compressed file format for tables, from Twitter and Cloudera in 2013, after Google's Dremel paper. Great for analytics and data lakes; not for changing single rows - which is what the table formats fix.
Four clicks. 1: the row layout fills in, reading by reading. 2: to average the power we sweep through all 18 values. 3: the column layout. 4: jump straight to the kW block - 6 of 18.
Three clicks: dictionary, then run-length, then a codec on top. The numbers underneath are measured live on the sensor readings - written to Parquet in memory just now.
Inside the file: row groups, one chunk per column, and a footer with min/max for every chunk. The reader reads the footer first, skips three of four row groups, reads one chunk out of sixteen.

Delta Lake in one slide. Born at Databricks, open-sourced 2019. The one idea: Parquet files plus a log of commits. It is the format under Databricks and under Fabric's OneLake, so the managed platforms from the last slides are already running on an open format.

Step 1. Creating the table writes no data, only the first log file: protocol and schema. Four panels: the SQL and the commit it writes on top; the files on disk and what a reader sees below (nothing yet).

Step 2. The Parquet file is written first, then one JSON file lists it. Until that commit lands, nobody sees the rows - that is the all-or-nothing guarantee. If the writer crashes before the commit, nothing happened.

Step 3. S1 dropped out at 12:15 and logged a zero. Parquet files can't be edited, so the file holding that row is rewritten without it: remove part-0001, add part-0002. part-0001 stays on disk (struck through), which is what makes time travel work, until VACUUM. Box: deletion vectors, what Databricks and Fabric do instead of rewriting.

Step 4. S2 was miscalibrated. An UPDATE is the same move as the DELETE: rewrite the affected file with the new values, commit remove + add. Four versions now, each one readable. Box: checkpoints - every 10 commits a Parquet snapshot of the whole log, so readers don't replay thousands of JSON files.

The real thing: the full v3 commit delta-rs wrote for the step-4 UPDATE. Three actions. commitInfo is for humans and audit; readVersion is how concurrency works - two writers race to create 00003.json, only one wins, the other checks for conflicts and retries as 00004. add carries min/max stats, so readers skip files from the log alone. remove is a tombstone. protocol and metaData only appear in the first commit, or when they change.

Schema evolution. Adding a column is one more commit with a new metaData action - no data file is rewritten; files written before it don't have the column, so readers fill in NULL. The flip side is enforcement: by default a write whose schema doesn't match fails. mergeSchema (Spark) or schema_mode='merge' (delta-rs) adds new columns as part of a write. Renames and drops need column mapping (name mode), which maps names to physical column ids - still metadata-only. Newer Delta versions also widen types (int to long) without a rewrite.

Iceberg gets the same guarantees with a tree instead of a log: catalog -> metadata file -> manifest list (one per snapshot) -> manifests -> Parquet files. A commit is one atomic pointer swap in the catalog. Born at Netflix. Differences on the right; in practice the choice usually follows your platform - Databricks and Fabric speak Delta, Snowflake and AWS lean Iceberg - and they are converging (UniForm; Databricks bought Tabular, the Iceberg founders' company).
Three shapes: a server for the app (Postgres), a library inside your process (DuckDB), a columnar server for real-time analytics (ClickHouse).
Live: edit the SQL - it runs inside this notebook's Python process, straight on the raw gzipped CSV. Then try SELECT * FROM gold: the dashboard's DataFrame is a table too.

Postgres: the default. Most used database in the Stack Overflow survey three years running; extensions make it a geo, vector or time-series database. Show https://db-engines.com/en/ranking if there's time. But it's a row store - remember the Parquet race.

ClickHouse when many users need sub-second dashboards on billions of rows, as data keeps arriving. Click for the MergeTree diagram, then four clicks: every INSERT writes a small sorted part and queries read all of them; a background merge combines them into one bigger part, and once it is ready queries switch to it; more inserts, more merges. Inserts stay cheap, and queries end up reading few big sorted parts.
Transformation: turning raw into the gold tables a dashboard needs.

Two styles, same job - pick by the team's skills more than by speed. SQL in the database: Postgres, ClickHouse or DuckDB do the work; dbt turns a folder of SELECT statements into a pipeline - ref() gives the order, plus tests, docs and lineage. Dataframes: pandas is the one everyone knows, Polars the fast modern one (Rust, lazy, all cores), Spark when it really needs a cluster - and Spark is also Scala, Java and R. The line is blurry: spark.sql, Polars' SQLContext, DuckDB querying a pandas or Polars frame in place.

PDS-H: Polars' TPC-H-derived benchmark - 22 analytical queries (joins, group-bys) at scale factor 10 (~10 GB) and 100 (~100 GB), on one big AWS machine (c7a.24xlarge, 96 vCPU, 192 GB), May 2025. Vendor-run, so a grain of salt - but it matches the independent ones. DuckDB and Polars are in the same league: seconds for 100 GB. PySpark is 10-30x slower on one machine - it pays for distribution it doesn't need. pandas is single-threaded and eager: ~100x slower, and out of memory at SF-100. Polars here is its streaming engine; in-memory Polars was 9.7 s and 152 s; Dask 46 s and 549 s. The other well-known one, DuckDB Labs' db-benchmark (ex H2O.ai), groupby on 50 GB on a 128-core box: DuckDB 21 s, Polars 75 s, pandas 822 s; Spark currently fails or isn't tested there. The point: most companies' data fits on one machine - Spark is for when it really doesn't.

ClickBench: published by ClickHouse, open, anyone can submit results. The dataset is one flat 'hits' table of anonymised web analytics (Yandex Metrica): 99,997,497 rows, 105 columns, ~14.8 GB as Parquet, ~70-75 GB as CSV. 43 dashboard-style queries: counts, group-bys, top-N, string filters. Score per query = (10 ms + time) / (10 ms + the fastest system's time), then a geometric mean; hot = the better of runs 2 and 3. On its default 16-vCPU / 32 GB machine, as of 20 Oct 2026: ClickHouse x3.1, DuckDB x6.0, Polars x6.6, Spark x153, plain PostgreSQL x6,588 - a row store with no indexes doing analytics. The very fastest are research engines like Umbra (about x1.4). Caveats: run by a vendor, numbers move as results are added, and one table of read-only queries is not your workload.
Serving: where people actually see the data.
The ecosystem as a spectrum: BI apps where you click, dashboards-as-code frameworks, chart libraries, and the new browser-native engines. Left is faster to start, right gives full control.
One example from each project's own gallery - just to show the range. Everything here is free and open source.

Be fair to Power BI: for business self-service, the semantic model and the Microsoft 365 integration it is genuinely hard to beat, and someone else runs it. Open source wins on cost at scale, visual freedom, version control and embedding. Pro is $14/user/month since April 2025; free viewers need F64 capacity.

Something I did not expect: coding agents are really good at dataviz. This is a dashboard Kurt Buhler built with Claude Code, comparing the steps counted by his watch and by his ring. Violin, swarm, slope chart, annotations - in a UI-driven tool that is days of fighting the tool, here you describe it and get Vega-Lite or D3 back. The quote is from his post about it.
Superset for data teams - Maxime Beauchemin started it at Airbnb, the same person who started Airflow. Metabase for business users: the easiest thing on this list to get running.

Press play: a D3 bar chart race over the same gold table as the dashboard. Hover a bar, click one to highlight it. You can't build this in a BI tool. It used to cost days of D3; with a coding assistant it is minutes - this one was written with one.

Top: every click is a round trip. Bottom: the engine is compiled to WebAssembly and downloaded once with the data; after that every interaction is local. Perspective, DuckDB-WASM, even Python itself via Pyodide - marimo can export this whole deck to run in the browser.

Live: the fleet's P&L - revenue from the grid settlement, every cost line from finance - pivoted in the browser by Perspective's WASM engine. Open the settings: split by plant or country, switch to a datagrid for a P&L table, filter a year.
Orchestration: something has to run all of this every day, in order, and retry what fails.
Airflow is the safe choice: everybody knows it, every cloud sells it managed. The DAG is Python, the UI shows every task of every run.

Dagster turns it around: instead of tasks you declare assets - the tables and files you want to exist - and the function that builds each one. The parameters are the upstream assets, so the graph and the lineage come for free, Dagster knows what is stale and rebuilds only that. dbt models and Airbyte syncs show up as assets in the same graph. The screenshots, click the dots: the asset graph, ingestion and dbt in one graph, a run, an asset's page. It has been growing fast: PyPI downloads went from about 1.4M a month in September 2024 to 8.2M in September 2026 (ClickPy) - downloads include CI, so it is a trend, not users - and about 15.8k GitHub stars. In July 2026 Prefect announced it is acquiring Dagster Labs: both products stay, Dagster keeps its name and its open-source licence.
Deployment: where all these tools actually run.

How Docker works, three clicks. A Dockerfile is a recipe: start from a base image, add what the app needs, say how to start it. 1: docker build makes an image - read-only layers, cached, so changing only your code rebuilds only the top layer. 2: docker push stores it in a registry - Docker Hub, GitHub, your cloud's. 3: docker run, on any machine with Docker, starts containers: isolated processes with their own files and network, sharing the host's kernel - lighter than VMs, they start in seconds. Same image everywhere: no more 'works on my machine'.

Technical detail, skip if needed. The whole Dockerfile for a marimo dashboard: a slim Python base, pip install the libraries, copy the app folder, expose marimo's port, run it. Build, run, open the browser. The same image goes to CI and production; a new version is a new tag, and rolling back is running the old one.

A real platform is more than one app: a database, Airflow, Superset. Each already ships an official image - you don't write Dockerfiles for them, only configuration. Click 1: on one machine, a compose.yaml lists the services, their settings, a shared network and a volume so the data survives restarts; docker compose up starts it all - often all a small team needs. Click 2: when one machine isn't enough, or mustn't be a single point of failure, Kubernetes runs the same images across several machines; Helm charts are ready-made installs for Airflow, Superset and Postgres.

Four clicks. You declare what should run, Kubernetes places the containers on the machines. A machine dies: its containers restart elsewhere. More users: more dashboard copies. New version: replaced one copy at a time, no downtime.
The last question of the talk: open source, or a managed platform?

Before the costs slide, a real comparison, from Adriano Sanges' talk at PyCon Italia 2026, 'The Modern Data Stack Is Overkill (Most of the Time)': the same workload priced on a Modern Data Stack and on a Python-native stack - DuckDB, dlt, dbt-core, Metabase or Lightdash. For a startup, 10 GB and 2 analysts: about 1,600 euro a month against 40, 40 times. Scale-up, 200 GB and 10 users: 6,400 against 235, 27 times. A real workload, 5 TB and 50 concurrent users: 25,000 against 4,000, still 6 times - there he swaps in ClickHouse and says ops complexity goes up. Numbers from public pricing, plus or minus 30%. The gap shrinks as you grow, and what you save in licences you partly pay in people - which is the next slide.

Costs. Open source has no licence fees, but you pay in development effort: running the infrastructure, and building and maintaining the software on top. If your organization is good at managing data with open-source tools, that effort turns into a competitive advantage. Managed: you pay licences plus usage (compute, storage, seats), at the vendor's prices - often in credits or capacity units that are hard to map to real cost - and they can go up: Power BI Pro went from $10 to $14 per user per month in April 2025.

Infrastructure. Open source vs managed often comes down to on-prem vs cloud: with your own data centre, open source runs on what you already have. In between there are managed versions of open-source tools. And open source is often a business model: release the software to get adoption, then sell consulting, support or a hosted version - ClickHouse, DuckDB's MotherDuck, Airflow's Astronomer, Superset's Preset.

Flexibility. Open source runs anywhere, so moving to another cloud means moving containers. You pick the best tool for each job instead of one vendor's bundle. And if a feature is missing you can build it, or pay someone to, instead of waiting for a vendor's roadmap. The quote is from the 2026 State of Open Source Report survey: avoiding vendor lock-in is one of the main reasons organizations adopt open source, cited by 55% of respondents.

Integration. A managed platform is one product: storage, pipelines, catalog and BI already talk to each other, so you get from raw data to a shared dashboard much faster. With open source, connecting the tools - one login, the same permissions everywhere, metadata flowing between them - is your job, and it's where much of the effort goes. For many corporations Microsoft is the deciding factor: they already live in Microsoft 365 and Entra ID, and Fabric and Power BI plug straight into those accounts, Teams, Excel and SharePoint.

Governance and compliance is where managed platforms shine: security, encryption, data masking and authentication built in, certifications that help with audits, and catalogs and lineage (Unity Catalog, Purview). Open source has the building blocks - Keycloak, OpenMetadata, DataHub, Postgres row-level security - but you set them up and maintain them. Same for operations: a vendor gives you support and SLAs, with open source your team does the upgrades, patches and incidents. And open source has risks too: Elasticsearch, Redis and Terraform all changed licence, and smaller projects can lose their maintainers.

Who usually goes open source. Organisations with their own infrastructure - data centres, ops teams, data that can't leave. Organisations where data engineering is a core competence and an edge - most of these tools were born there: Airflow and Superset at Airbnb, Iceberg at Netflix, Presto at Facebook. And academia: openness to share and reproduce, tight budgets, own clusters - Postgres and Spark came out of Berkeley, DuckDB out of CWI.
Thank you. Two QR codes: the left one opens the GitHub repo - the slides, the dashboard and the data generator, everything from today. The right one is the feedback form, it takes a minute.
Resources, if you want to go further: two books, the articles and benchmarks quoted in the talk, and the docs and specs of the formats we looked at. Then questions.
